question: A security lead configures a project-level deny rule Bash(aws *) to block all AWS CLI usage from Claude Code. A developer later adds an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls) to their local settings so they can list bucket contents. When the developer runs aws s3 ls in a session, what happens?
options: A) The command triggers a one-time confirmation prompt, because Claude Code merges conflicting rules of equal specificity into an ask decision
B) The command runs without a prompt, because local settings always override project settings regardless of whether the rule is allow or deny
C) The command runs without a prompt, because the more specific allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls) takes precedence over the broader deny pattern Bash(aws *)
D) The command is blocked, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and a broad deny cannot carry allowlist exceptions from a narrower allow rule
correct_answers: D) The command is blocked, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and a broad deny cannot carry allowlist exceptions from a narrower allow rule
explanations: Incorrect. There is no rule-merging step that converts a deny/allow conflict into an ask prompt; the deny rule wins outright and the command is blocked with no prompt.

Incorrect. Local settings can add stricter or looser rules within their own scope, but they do not grant an exception to a deny rule defined at a different scope, since deny rules from any scope are evaluated before allow rules.
Incorrect. Specificity does not override the deny-first evaluation order; a narrower allow rule matching the same call as a broader deny rule still loses to the deny rule.

Correct. Rules are evaluated in the fixed order deny, then ask, then allow, and rule specificity does not change that order, so a broad deny rule like Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call even when a narrower allow rule also matches.
